```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
library(nnet)
library(AER)
```

## Learning Objectives

If provided with the assumptions of a baseline category logit model,

- Interpret the coefficients
- Interpret the results of a hypothesis test


## Lesson

### Overview

In the baseline category logit model, we assume that
for each $m\in\{1,2,\dotsc,M-1\}$,
$$
\log \left(\frac{\pi_{im}}{\pi_{iM}}\right) = \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{ip} \text{.}
$$
In words, we assume that the log risk ratio comparing level $m$
to level $M$ is a linear function of the covariates.

### Interpretation

How do we interpret the coefficients?
Let's start with the intercept.
Suppose all the covariates are equal to zero.
Then
$$
\begin{align*}
\log \left(\frac{\pi_{im}}{\pi_{iM}}\right) &= \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} (0) + \cdots + \beta_{pm} (0) \\
\log \left(\frac{\pi_{im}}{\pi_{iM}}\right) &= \beta_{0m}  \\
\frac{\pi_{im}}{\pi_{iM}} &= \exp\left(\beta_{0m}\right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$
So, $\exp\left(\beta_{0m}\right)$ is the ratio of the risk of level $m$
to the risk of level $M$ when all the covariates equal zero.

What about non-intercept coefficients?
Suppose observations $i$ and $j$ differ only in that $X_{i1} = x + 1$
and $X_{j1} = x$.
Then
$$
\begin{align*}
\log \left(\frac{\pi_{im}}{\pi_{iM}}\right) - \log \left(\frac{\pi_{jm}}{\pi_{jM}}\right) &= \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{ip} - \left(\beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} X_{j1} + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{jp}\right) \\
\log \left(\frac{\pi_{im}/\pi_{iM}}{\pi_{jm}/\pi_{jM}}\right)  &= \beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} (x + 1) + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{ip} - \left(\beta_{0m} + \beta_{1m} x + \cdots + \beta_{pm} X_{ip}\right) \\
\log \left(\frac{\pi_{im}/\pi_{iM}}{\pi_{jm}/\pi_{jM}}\right) &= \beta_{1m} \\
\frac{\pi_{im}/\pi_{iM}}{\pi_{jm}/\pi_{jM}} &= \exp\left(\beta_{1m}\right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$
In words, the ratio of the risk of category $m$ to the risk of category $M$
among observations with $X_{i1} = x + 1$ is $\exp\left(\beta_{1m}\right)$ times
the same ratio among observations with $X_{i1} = x$,
holding all else constant.

I know that's a lot of words.
Interpreting the coefficients in regression with a categorical outcome
always results in a lot of words.

### Hypothesis Testing

As always, the default null hypothesis for a test involving a regression
coefficient is that the coefficient equals zero.
Here, as in logistic, Poisson, and Cox regression,
we are exponentiating our coefficients,
so the null hypothesis is that the exponentiated coefficient equals 1.
For the baseline category logit model,
$\beta_{0m} = 0$ would imply that
the risk of level $m$ is equal
to the risk of level $M$ when all the covariates equal zero.
In contrast,
$\beta_{1m} = 0$ would imply that
the ratio of the risk of category $m$ to the risk of category $M$
among observations with $X_{i1} = x + 1$ is equal to
the same ratio among observations with $X_{i1} = x$.

### Example

```{r}
d_student <- Lock5Data::StudentSurvey
```

Let's look at a data set containing survey responses from students
in introductory statistics courses.
Our outcome will be the student's preferred award from among these
three options: Academy Award, Nobel Prize, or Olympic Medal.
For explanatory variables, we'll use
sex (`F` is female, `M` is male),
hours of exercise per week,
hours of TV viewing per week,
and combined verbal and math SAT score.

```{r}
#| echo: true
# The multinom function is from the package nnet
mod_01 <- multinom(formula = Award ~ Sex + Exercise + TV + SAT,
                   data = d_student)
summary(mod_01)
exp(summary(mod_01)$coefficients)
```

**Interpretations**

- 0.143208: Among females who don't exercise or watch TV
and who scored a zero on the SAT,
the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize is 86% lower than
the probability of preferring an Academy Award.
- 9.652715: Among females who don't exercise or watch TV
and who scored a zero on the SAT,
the probability of preferring an Olympic medal is 9.65 times
the probability of preferring an Academy Award.
- 1.802041: The ratio of the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize
to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
among males is 1.8 times the same ratio among females,
holding all else constant.
- 2.333026: The ratio of the probability of preferring an Olympic Medal
to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
among males is 2.33 times the same ratio among females,
holding all else constant.
- 0.9955136: The ratio of the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize
to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
among students who exercise $x+1$ hours per week
is 0.45% lower than the same ratio among students who exercise $x$ hours per week,
holding all else constant.
- 1.1717084: The ratio of the probability of preferring an Olympic Medal
to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
among students who exercise $x+1$ hours per week
is 17% greater than the same ratio among students who exercise $x$ hours per week,
holding all else constant.
- 0.9530915: The ratio of the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize
to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
among students who watch $x+1$ hours of TV per week
is 5% lower than the same ratio among students who watch $x$ hours of TV per week,
holding all else constant.
- 1.0036990: The ratio of the probability of preferring an Olympic Medal
to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
among students who watch $x+1$ hours of TV per week
is 0.37% higher than the same ratio among students who watch $x$ hours of TV per week,
holding all else constant.
- 1.0029547: The ratio of the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize
to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
among students who scored $x+1$ on the SAT
is 0.29% higher than the same ratio among students who scored $x$ on the SAT,
holding all else constant.
- 0.9980527: The ratio of the probability of preferring an Olympic Medal
to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
among students who scored $x+1$ on the SAT
is 0.19% lower than the same ratio among students who scored $x$ on the SAT,
holding all else constant.


**Hypothesis Tests**

```{r}
#| echo: true
# The coeftest function is from the package AER
coeftest(mod_01)
```

For these tests, we'll use $\alpha = 0.05$.

- There is a statistically significant difference between the following:
  - The probability of preferring a Nobel Prize and
  the probability of preferring an Academy Award,
  among females who don't exercise or watch TV
  and who scored a zero on the SAT.
  - The ratio of the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize
  to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
  among students who scored $x+1$ on the SAT
  and the same ratio among students who scored $x$ on the SAT,
  holding all else constant.
  - The probability of preferring an Olympic medal and
  the probability of preferring an Academy Award,
  among females who don't exercise or watch TV
  and who scored a zero on the SAT.
  - The ratio of the probability of preferring an Olympic Medal
  to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
  among males and the same ratio among females,
  holding all else constant.
  - The ratio of the probability of preferring an Olympic Medal
  to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
  among students who exercise $x+1$ hours per week
  and the same ratio among students who exercise $x$ hours per week,
  holding all else constant.
  - The ratio of the probability of preferring an Olympic Medal
  to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
  among students who scored $x+1$ on the SAT
  and the same ratio among students who scored $x$ on the SAT,
  holding all else constant.
- There is not a statistically significant difference between the following:
  - The ratio of the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize
  to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
  among males and the same ratio among females,
  holding all else constant.
  - The ratio of the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize
  to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
  among students who exercise $x+1$ hours per week
  and the same ratio among students who exercise $x$ hours per week,
  holding all else constant.
  - The ratio of the probability of preferring a Nobel Prize
  to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
  among students who watch $x+1$ hours of TV per week
  and the same ratio among students who watch $x$ hours of TV per week,
  holding all else constant.
  - The ratio of the probability of preferring an Olympic Medal
  to the probability of preferring an Academy Award
  among students who watch $x+1$ hours of TV per week
  and the same ratio among students who watch $x$ hours of TV per week,
  holding all else constant.


## Problems

### Problem 1

```{r}
d_iris <- Lock5Data::FisherIris
d_iris$Type <- relevel(x = d_iris$Type,
                       ref = "Versicolor")
d_iris$PetalWidth_13 <- d_iris$PetalWidth - 13
d_iris$PetalLength_44 <- d_iris$PetalLength - 44
d_iris$SepalWidth_28 <- d_iris$SepalWidth - 28
d_iris$SepalLength_59 <- d_iris$SepalLength - 59
```


Let's look at a famous data set from the 1936 paper
"[The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-1809.1936.tb02137.x)."
Each observation is an iris (flower);
the outcome is species, with three options:
Setosa, Virginica, and Versicolor.
These are the explanatory variables:

- Petal length in mm.
- Petal width in mm.
- Sepal length in mm.
- Sepal width in mm.

```{r}
mod_02 <- multinom(formula = Type ~ PetalLength_44 + PetalWidth_13 + SepalLength_59 + SepalWidth_28,
                   data = d_iris)
summary(mod_02)
```

#### Part (a)

Interpret the coefficients in real-world terms.

```{r}
#| echo: true
exp(summary(mod_02)$coefficients)
```

#### Part (b)



Interpret the results of the hypothesis tests associated with the coefficients.

